title: What the Discovery Navigator is
description: The navigator starts from seed questions and expands outward: following links, generating follow-up queries, and growing a knowledge graph of what it finds. Unlike a search box that answers one query, it runs an expedition — planning where to look next based on what it just learned, until its budget runs out or the question is answered.

demo.title: Runnable code demo — What the Discovery Navigator is

architecture: An expedition planner maintains a frontier of unexplored leads ranked by expected gain; workers execute searches and fetches; a graph store accumulates findings; a budget ledger stops expansion when resources are spent.

title: Expedition and lead data model
description: Every expedition is a record: seeds, budget, strategy, and the full trail of what was tried and found. Every lead is a record too: where it came from, what it might contain, its estimated cost, and its estimated gain. This trail is what makes discovery reproducible and auditable — anyone can replay the expedition.

title: Expected-gain ranking algorithm
description: The frontier can hold thousands of leads; the navigator must pick the next one wisely. Each lead gets an expected-gain score from features like source reliability, topical novelty, and past yield of similar leads. The ranking is learned from the expedition's own history — leads like ones that paid off before rank higher.

demo.title: Runnable code demo — Expected-gain ranking algorithm

architecture: Feature extractor over leads; online learning model updating weights as findings arrive; ranker serving the top lead on demand; exploration bonus for under-sampled lead types.

title: Recursive query generation algorithm
description: Each finding suggests new questions: a paper's references become new searches, an unfamiliar term becomes a definition query, a dataset mention becomes a retrieval task. The generator turns findings into queries using templates and learned patterns, then deduplicates them against everything already tried so the expedition never chases its own tail.

title: Stopping reasoning: knowing when to quit
description: The hardest part of discovery is stopping. The navigator tracks marginal gain per unit of budget: when new leads consistently yield less than a threshold, or the budget ledger empties, the expedition ends and reports what it found and what remains unexplored. Quitting well is a feature, not a failure.

title: Failure modes: loops, traps, and budget fires
description: Discovery fails in known ways: crawler traps that generate infinite leads, query generators that drift off-topic, budgets burned on one mega-source. The navigator defends with lead deduplication, topic-drift monitors, per-source spend caps, and circuit breakers that pause a worker burning budget with no yield.

description: Big expeditions run as fleets: a planner partitions the frontier by source and topic, workers on many machines execute in parallel, and findings stream back into one graph. title: Security: safe discovery at scale
description: A navigator that fetches the whole web will eventually fetch something malicious or private. Sandboxed fetching, content-type restrictions, credential isolation per source, and audit logs of every fetch keep discovery safe. Private sources are only touched with explicit permission scopes.
